nameStory: The 'sea heart' name comes from the distinctive heart-shaped seeds that wash up on beaches around the world after drifting across oceans. These remarkable seeds can float for years in ocean currents, earning them the romantic French name 'cœur de la mer' (heart of the sea). Beachcombers have treasured these natural hearts for centuries, often keeping them as good luck charms.
description: Sea heart is a massive tropical vine (called a liana) from the pea family that produces the largest seed pods of any legume in the world. In its native range of Central America, the Caribbean, and parts of South America and Africa, it climbs high into forest canopies with thick, woody stems. The plant is famous for its huge, flat seed pods that can reach several feet long, containing large, heart-shaped seeds that eventually break free and travel the world's oceans. In New England, you won't find the living plant, but you might discover its distinctive seeds washed up on our beaches.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Large, flattened, distinctly heart-shaped seeds about 2-3 inches across with a smooth, glossy brown surface that feels like polished wood. The seed has a prominent 'eye' or scar where it attached to the pod.

idTips.label: Seed Texture
idTips.description: Seeds feel surprisingly heavy and dense for their size, with a hard, waterproof coating that's been polished smooth by months or years of tumbling in ocean waves.

idTips.label: Beach Context
idTips.description: Found among other drift seeds and marine debris on beaches, often mixed with seaweed, shells, and driftwood after storms or high tides.

idTips.label: Color Variation
idTips.description: Fresh seeds are rich chocolate brown and glossy, while older beach specimens may be faded to lighter brown or gray but retain their distinctive heart shape.

habitat: In New England, sea heart seeds are found washed up on Atlantic-facing beaches, particularly after storms or during spring tides when ocean debris accumulates on shore. Look for them among the wrack line (the ridge of seaweed and debris left by high tide) on sandy or rocky beaches from Maine to Connecticut. The Gulf Stream current system occasionally carries these seeds north to our shores from their tropical origins.

seasonality.spring: Spring storms and high tides may bring fresh sea heart seeds to New England beaches. This is often the best time to search as winter storms have stirred up ocean debris.
seasonality.summer: Seeds found in summer have usually been on the beach longer and may be more weathered. Beach combing after summer storms can yield discoveries.
seasonality.fall: Hurricane season can bring tropical drift items northward, potentially depositing sea heart seeds on New England shores along with other storm debris.
seasonality.winter: Winter nor'easters may uncover buried seeds or bring new ones ashore. Seeds are most visible when beaches are stripped of summer sand buildup.

funFact: Sea heart seeds can survive floating in ocean currents for up to 15 years while remaining viable enough to sprout if they wash up in the right tropical location - making them some of nature's most accomplished long-distance travelers, literally crossing entire oceans to colonize new shores.
confusionNotes: Sea heart seeds might be confused with other large drift seeds or even beach stones, but their distinctive heart shape and woody texture make them unique. Unlike rounded sea beans or beach glass, sea hearts have that unmistakable flattened heart profile with a pointed bottom and curved top.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'sea beans,' these seeds come from a vine, not a bean plant in the garden sense. The term 'drift seed' is more accurate for these ocean travelers. Many cultures consider finding a sea heart to be extremely lucky, and they've been used in folk medicine and as decorative items for centuries.
compareHints: Sea heart is the only species in its genus found (as drift seeds) in New England waters. Compared to other legume seeds that might wash ashore, sea hearts are distinctively large and heart-shaped rather than round or oval. Other 'sea beans' from tropical drift tend to be smaller, rounder, and lack the pronounced heart outline that makes Entada gigas seeds unmistakable.
